title: Take away the opinion
hookLine: take away "I've been harmed," and the harm is gone (Meditations 4.7)

cards: A friend forgets your birthday. That's the event. Within an hour it has a title: they don't care about me.
By evening it has a sequel: nobody really does. The event took one second. The title has been running for days.
A grievance can work like this: a small fact, and a big label stuck on top. Marcus Aurelius wrote two short sentences about peeling the label off. Today: take away the opinion.

teach.b: In the seventh entry of book four Marcus writes, in effect: take away your opinion, and the complaint I have been harmed is taken away. Take away the complaint, and the harm is taken away.
Three links: the opinion makes the complaint, the complaint makes the harm. What does he mean by harm? This is not a claim that broken bones don't hurt or that injustice isn't real.

teach.h: WHAT DOESN'T MAKE YOU WORSE, ISN'T HARM.
teach.b: What doesn't make a person worse, he says, doesn't make their life worse, and doesn't harm them, outside or in. For a Stoic, the only real harm is to your character.
In those terms, a forgotten birthday can't make anyone less honest or less kind. Only the response can.
So the work is to notice where the event ends and the label begins. They forgot: event. They don't care about me: label.
Take the label off and you're left with something smaller and truer, something you can deal with. Maybe with a phone call.
Look back at the week. Tools ready. Help yourself now.
And now, take away the label, which sits underneath several of the others, since obstacles, strangers and cravings can all arrive with a label already attached.

how: Some readers of Marcus Aurelius practice Meditations 4.7 by separating what happened from the label they've put on it, then setting the label down.

o: a Roman lawyer who taught people to sue for every insult
the emperor who said remove the opinion and the harm goes too
a Roman judge who ruled that hurt feelings were crimes

games.q: take away the label — tap the pairs.

s: Marcus says injustice and pain aren't real
his claim is narrower: only what makes you worse truly harms you.
in the next entry Marcus says what doesn't make you worse doesn't harm you
Marcus links opinion, complaint and harm in a chain
take away the first, and the others go with it.

games.q: a coworker repeats your idea in a meeting, and the boss praises them. what fits Meditations 4.7?
o: file it under betrayal and stay cold.
split the event from the label, then decide what to do.
games.why: Marcus removes the opinion first. without the label, you can respond to the event, maybe by speaking up calmly.

practice: Bring to mind one grievance you've been carrying, small or medium, and say in plain words what actually happened. Then notice the label you added, disrespect, betrayal, typical, and for this breath set it down beside you.
Look at the event without it: is there anything there that makes you worse, unless you let it?

wordCard.voice: Marcus, who said take away the opinion and the complaint goes, take away the complaint and the harm goes too. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek, 'I have been harmed': the complaint Marcus says to take away in 4.7.

carryVoice: Your line: take away the label. What happened is one thing; what I call it is another. Another week, done.
